mvt.prehistoric.o.0.n: Chauvet-Pont-d’Arc cave, Ardèche (French state, Ministry of Culture)
mvt.prehistoric.o.0.what: the horse panels, among them the Panel of the Large Engraved Horse, in situ; the cave is closed and shown in replica
mvt.prehistoric.o.1.n: Lascaux, Montignac, Dordogne (French state, Ministry of Culture)
mvt.prehistoric.o.1.what: the Hall of the Bulls, in situ in the closed cave, with the replicas including Lascaux IV
mvt.prehistoric.o.2.n: Museo Nacional y Centro de Investigación de Altamira, Santillana del Mar (Spanish Ministry of Culture)
mvt.prehistoric.o.2.what: the polychrome bison ceiling, in the original cave and in the Neocave replica painted with Palaeolithic techniques
mvt.prehistoric.sync: Modern humans reached Europe after about 45,000 years ago, and Neanderthals vanish from the record around 40,000 years ago. At the glacial maximum, 26,500 to 19,000 years ago, ice covered most of northern Europe and the sea stood 110 to 120 metres lower; people crossed from Beringia into the Americas by about 15,000 years ago. The Löwenmensch ivory figure of 40,000 to 35,000 years ago and Spanish cave art of 40,000 years ago are Europe’s oldest images; the Sulawesi caves are older still.
mvt.egypt.o.0.what: King Menkaura and queen, greywacke, 2490–2472 BC, found at the Menkaura valley temple at Giza in 1910 and assigned to the museum in 1911 (acc. 11.1738)
mvt.egypt.o.1.what: The Seated Scribe (E 3023), found by Mariette at Saqqara on 19 November 1850
mvt.egypt.o.2.n: Neues Museum, Berlin (Ägyptisches Museum und Papyrussammlung)
mvt.egypt.o.2.what: the bust of Nefertiti, c. 1340 BC, from Tell el-Amarna, found in 1912, in the North Dome Room
mvt.egypt.sync: Egypt was united about 3150 BC, and the Giza pyramids rose in the Old Kingdom (c. 2686–2181 BC) while Sumerian and Akkadian cities ruled Mesopotamia and traded with the Nile. Drought around 2200 BC brought famine and strife. The Hyksos held the Delta from c. 1785 BC; the New Kingdom, from 1549 BC, reached from Syria to the Fourth Cataract, Akhenaten moved his court to Amarna c. 1350 BC, and Ramesses II sealed the first recorded peace treaty with the Hittites c. 1258 BC. Persia, Alexander and Rome followed.
mvt.greekroman.o.0.what: about half the surviving Parthenon sculptures: 15 metopes, 17 pediment figures and 75 metres of the frieze
mvt.greekroman.o.1.what: the other half of the Parthenon sculptures, in the museum opened in 2009
mvt.greekroman.o.2.what: the Doryphoros, Roman marble copy of 120–50 BC after Polykleitos
mvt.greekroman.o.3.what: the Augustus of Prima Porta, early first century AD, found in Livia’s villa on the Via Flaminia
mvt.greekroman.o.4.what: the Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory of Samothrace
mvt.greekroman.sync: Homer’s poems and the first Olympiad of 776 BC open the age; colonies grew into city-states, Rome expelled its kings in 509 BC, and the Persian Wars of 499–449 BC left Athens heading the Delian League until Sparta won in 404 BC. Alexander died in 323 BC and his generals divided the East, where Koine Greek became the common tongue. Rome won the Punic Wars, took Greece in 146 BC and became an empire under Augustus in 27 BC; the Theodosian decrees of 393 ended the imperial cult.
mvt.byzantine.o.0.what: the encaustic Christ Pantokrator of the mid-sixth century, the earliest surviving image of Christ as ruler of all
mvt.byzantine.o.1.n: Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, Moscow (Russian Orthodox Church)
mvt.byzantine.o.1.what: the Virgin of Vladimir, painted in Constantinople in the twelfth century, transferred from the State Tretyakov Gallery on 3 April 2026 for 49 years of church use
mvt.byzantine.o.2.n: Trinity Lavra of St Sergius, Sergiyev Posad (Russian Orthodox Church)
mvt.byzantine.o.2.what: Rublev’s Trinity (1411 or 1425–27), returned to the iconostasis of the Trinity Cathedral in 2024 after 93 years in the Tretyakov; its condition was reported critical in September 2026
mvt.byzantine.sync: Constantine founded Constantinople in 330, and Justinian (527–65) rebuilt Hagia Sophia after the Nika riots of 532. Arab armies took Syria and Egypt by 642; Leo III removed the Christ icon over his gate in 726, and icons were restored at Nicaea in 787. Papal legates laid a bull of excommunication on Hagia Sophia’s altar in 1054, Manzikert opened Anatolia to the Turks in 1071, the Fourth Crusade sacked the city in 1204 and the Ottomans took it in 1453. Moscow, victor at Kulikovo in 1380, inherited the icon.
mvt.gothic.o.0.what: the central panel, lower panels and back of Duccio’s Maestà (1308–11), installed in the cathedral on 9 June 1311
mvt.gothic.o.1.n: National Gallery, London; National Gallery of Art, Washington; Frick Collection, New York; Thyssen-Bornemisza, Madrid; Kimbell, Fort Worth
mvt.gothic.o.1.what: the dispersed predella and pinnacle panels of the Maestà
mvt.gothic.o.2.what: Simone Martini and Lippo Memmi’s Annunciation with Saints Ansanus and Margaret, 1333, painted for Siena Cathedral (inv. 1890 nos. 451–453)
mvt.gothic.o.3.what: Gentile da Fabriano’s Adoration of the Magi, 1423, commissioned by Palla Strozzi for Santa Trinita (inv. 1890 no. 8364)
mvt.gothic.sync: The Great Famine of 1315–17 came first; the Black Death from 1347 killed a third to three fifths of Europe, and by about 1420 repeated plagues had cut its population to perhaps a third of the level of 1300. The Hundred Years’ War ran from 1337, with firearms at Crécy in 1346; the papacy sat at Avignon from 1309 to 1376 and rival popes split the Church from 1378 to 1417. Florence grew rich on bills of exchange and double-entry bookkeeping, and Dante began the Comedy around 1310.
mvt.earlyren.o.0.what: Masaccio’s Holy Trinity fresco, c. 1426–28, in the Dominican church
mvt.earlyren.o.1.what: Piero della Francesca’s Flagellation of Christ, 1459–60
mvt.earlyren.sync: Humanists such as Poggio Bracciolini hunted Latin manuscripts in monastic libraries, and Greek texts arrived with the scholars who fled Constantinople after the Ottomans took it in 1453. Movable type spread from a single shop in Mainz around 1440 to some 270 cities, which had printed more than 20 million volumes by 1500. Lorenzo de’ Medici (1449–92) ruled Florence as patron of Botticelli, Leonardo and the young Michelangelo, Matthias Corvinus made Buda a Renaissance court, and Lisbon’s captains worked down the African coast toward India.
mvt.northernren.o.0.what: the Ghent Altarpiece of Hubert and Jan van Eyck, completed 1432, in the principal chapel
mvt.northernren.o.1.what: Rogier van der Weyden’s Descent from the Cross, c. 1435, in the Prado since 1939
mvt.northernren.sync: Jan Hus had burned at Constance in 1415, and on 31 October 1517 Luther posted his theses against indulgences at Wittenberg; he refused to recant at Worms in 1521. The Peasants’ War of 1524–25 ended at Frankenhausen, Zwingli fell in battle in 1531, the protest at Speyer in 1529 gave Protestants their name, and the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 let each prince choose his faith. Luther wrote a fifth of everything printed in Germany in the century’s first third; Antwerp fell to Philip II’s army in 1585.
mvt.highren.o.0.what: the Mona Lisa, c. 1503–17, property of the French Republic and on view since 1797
mvt.highren.o.1.n: Sistine Chapel, Vatican Museums, Vatican City
mvt.highren.o.1.what: Michelangelo’s ceiling frescoes of 1508–12, commissioned by Julius II
mvt.highren.o.2.n: Apostolic Palace, Vatican City (Stanza della Segnatura)
mvt.highren.o.2.what: Raphael’s School of Athens, 1509–11, in the Stanze di Raffaello
mvt.highren.sync: Charles VIII of France crossed the Alps in September 1494 and was in Rome by the year’s end, and for a generation French and Habsburg armies fought over Italy. Francis I routed the Swiss at Marignano in 1515; at Pavia in February 1525 he was beaten and carried captive to Spain. In May 1527 unpaid imperial troops, many of them Lutherans, sacked Rome and besieged Clement VII in Castel Sant’Angelo, while Luther’s theses of 1517 had split the Church in Germany. Cambrai in 1529 sealed Habsburg rule.
mvt.mannerism.o.0.what: Pontormo’s Deposition from the Cross, 1525–28, above the chapel altar
mvt.mannerism.o.1.what: Parmigianino’s Madonna with the Long Neck, 1534–40, unfinished at his death, on view since 1948
mvt.mannerism.o.2.what: Bronzino’s Allegory with Venus and Cupid, c. 1545, in the collection since 1860
mvt.mannerism.sync: Leo X’s indulgences for St Peter’s had provoked Luther, and Paul III answered with the Council of Trent, which met from 13 December 1545 to 4 December 1563. The Jesuits were recognised in 1540, the Index of forbidden books first appeared in 1559, and the Inquisition summoned Veronese to explain his Last Supper. Lepanto followed in 1571, the French wars of religion ran from 1562 to the Edict of Nantes in 1598, and Antwerp fell to Philip II’s general Farnese in 1585.
mvt.baroque.o.0.what: Caravaggio’s The Calling of St Matthew, in the church for which it was painted
mvt.baroque.o.2.what: Bernini’s Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, 1647–52, in the Cornaro Chapel
mvt.baroque.o.3.what: Rubens’s The Four Continents, c. 1615, and Van Dyck’s Samson and Delilah, c. 1630
mvt.baroque.o.4.what: Caravaggio’s Death of the Virgin, c. 1606, and Rubens’s Marie de’ Medici cycle
mvt.baroque.sync: The Bohemian Revolt of 1618 began the Thirty Years’ War, and the Peace of Westphalia of 1648 ended it and Spain’s day as a great power. Galileo came to Rome for his trial before the Inquisition in 1633, Charles I was executed in 1649, and Newton published the Principia in 1687. The Manchu took China in 1644, Tokugawa Ieyasu became shōgun in 1603, and the Taj Mahal rose at Agra from 1632. Louis XIV reigned from 1643 to 1715 and enlarged Versailles from 1661.
mvt.dutchgolden.o.0.what: Rembrandt’s The Night Watch, 1642, and Vermeer’s The Milkmaid, c. 1660
mvt.dutchgolden.o.1.what: Vermeer’s View of Delft, c. 1661, Rembrandt’s The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp, 1632, and Fabritius’s The Goldfinch, 1654
mvt.dutchgolden.o.3.n: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
mvt.dutchgolden.o.3.what: Vermeer’s Woman with a Water Jug, c. 1660
mvt.dutchgolden.sync: The Dutch were still at war with Spain until the Peace of Westphalia closed the Eighty Years’ War in 1648. The Dutch East India Company, formed in 1602 by merging rival traders, razed Jayakarta and built Batavia on it in 1619, and a Dutch fleet broke a Spanish one at the Downs in 1639. Kepler began on the elliptical orbits in 1605 and Galileo was tried in 1633. England fought its civil war from 1642, and Louis XIV invaded the Republic in 1672.
mvt.rococo.o.2.what: Chardin’s Still Life with Glass Flask and Fruit, c. 1728
mvt.rococo.o.3.what: Vigée Le Brun’s Self-Portrait in a Straw Hat, c. 1783
mvt.rococo.o.4.n: Museu Nacional d’Art de Catalunya, Barcelona
mvt.rococo.o.4.what: Quentin de La Tour’s Portrait of Pierre-Louis Laideguive, c. 1761
mvt.rococo.sync: The death of Louis XIV in 1715 opened the ‘short’ eighteenth century that ran to the Revolution. Most of Europe fought the War of the Austrian Succession from 1740 to 1748, and the Seven Years’ War spread across the world from 1756 to 1763. Diderot’s Encyclopédie appeared from 1751, Catherine the Great took the Russian throne in 1762, and James Watt improved Newcomen’s steam engine in 1765. The Qianlong Emperor ruled China from 1735, while the Mughal empire broke apart after Aurangzeb’s death in 1707.
mvt.neoclassicism.o.0.what: David’s Oath of the Horatii and The Coronation of Napoleon, and Ingres’s Grande Odalisque
mvt.neoclassicism.o.1.n: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
mvt.neoclassicism.o.1.what: David’s The Death of Socrates, 1787, and Mengs’s portrait of Winckelmann, c. 1777
mvt.neoclassicism.o.2.what: Benjamin West’s The Death of General Wolfe, 1770
mvt.neoclassicism.o.3.what: Ingres’s Napoleon on His Imperial Throne, 1806
mvt.neoclassicism.o.4.what: Copley’s A Boy with a Flying Squirrel, 1765
mvt.neoclassicism.sync: The American Revolutionary War ran from 1775 to 1783, and the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence in Philadelphia in 1776. Watt’s improved steam engines were installed from 1776. The Bastille fell on 14 July 1789, and Napoleon won his first battle at Montenotte in 1796 and took power on 18 Brumaire 1799. The partitions of Poland ended the Commonwealth by 1795, Cook mapped the Pacific, and the Napoleonic Wars ran from 1803 to Waterloo.
mvt.romanticism.o.0.what: Géricault’s The Raft of the Medusa, 1819, and Delacroix’s Liberty Leading the People, 1830
mvt.romanticism.o.2.what: Goya’s The Third of May 1808, painted 1814, and Saturn Devouring His Son, c. 1820
mvt.romanticism.o.3.what: Caspar David Friedrich’s The Abbey in the Oakwood, c. 1810
mvt.romanticism.o.4.what: Brullov’s The Last Day of Pompeii, c. 1830, and Aivazovsky’s The Ninth Wave, 1850
mvt.romanticism.sync: The Napoleonic Wars ran from 1803 until Napoleon’s defeat at Waterloo, and the Congress of Vienna redrew the borders after him. The first steam locomotive ran in 1804 and the Stockton and Darlington, the first public railway, opened in 1825; Niépce made the first photograph in 1827. The July Revolution of 1830 overthrew the Bourbons, Britain fought the First Opium War from 1839, and the revolutions of 1848 shook Europe in the year Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto.
mvt.realism.o.0.what: Courbet’s A Burial at Ornans, c. 1850, and Millet’s The Gleaners, 1857
mvt.realism.o.2.what: Winslow Homer’s After the Hurricane, Bahamas, 1899, a work of the American realism of the same decades
mvt.realism.sync: Louis-Philippe ruled France from the July Revolution of 1830 until the February barricades of 1848, when Louis-Napoleon was elected president; he made himself Napoleon III in 1852 and set Haussmann to rebuild Paris from 1853. Britain, France and the Ottomans fought Russia in the Crimea in 1853–56. Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, Russia abolished serfdom in 1861 and America fought its Civil War from 1861 to 1865. Napoleon III fell with the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71.
mvt.peredvizhniki.o.0.what: Repin’s realist paintings: Western painting names the Russian Museum, with the Hermitage, as the chief Russian repository of his work; the Mikhailovsky Palace became the museum in 1895
mvt.peredvizhniki.sync: Russia abolished serfdom in 1861, and the great novels came out beside the Wanderers’ shows: Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment in 1866 and The Brothers Karamazov in 1879–80, Tolstoy’s War and Peace in 1869. Mendeleev presented the periodic table on 6 March 1869. Nicholas II was crowned in Moscow in 1896, Bloody Sunday opened the revolution of 1905, the Bolsheviks took power in 1917, and the capital moved from Petrograd to Moscow in 1918.
mvt.prerapha.sync: Victoria had reigned since 1837. The revolutions of 1848 shook Europe, and on 10 April that year the Chartists held a ‘monster’ rally on Kennington Common. The Brotherhood first showed in May 1849, Millais’s Isabella at the Royal Academy, and the Great Exhibition opened in the Crystal Palace on 1 May 1851. Britain fought in the Crimea in 1853–56, Dickens published Bleak House in 1853 and Hard Times in 1854, and Darwin’s On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859.
mvt.ukiyoe.o.0.what: a holding of Japanese prints and related items numbering more than 100,000
mvt.ukiyoe.o.1.what: a museum of ukiyo-e prints, named on the Wikipedia page among the places that hold them
mvt.ukiyoe.sync: Tokugawa Ieyasu became shōgun in 1603 and made Edo the seat of government; it grew from about 1,800 people to more than a million. From 1790 every print needed a censor’s seal, and Utamaro was jailed in 1804 for prints of Hideyoshi; the Tenpō Reforms of 1841–43 banned courtesans and actors, so artists turned to landscape. Perry reached Edo in 1853, the Convention of Kanagawa opened Japan in 1854, and the Meiji Restoration of 1868 and the Boshin War ended the shogunate.
mvt.chineseink.sync: The Jin moved their capital to Zhongdu, today’s Beijing, in 1153, and Zhu Xi (1130–1200) made the neo-Confucian synthesis whose commentaries set the civil-service examinations from 1313 to 1905. Kublai Khan began Dadu in 1267 and made it the capital of all China in 1279; Marco Polo lived some 17 years in his lands. The Yongle Emperor moved the Ming capital to Beijing in 1421, the Manchus took the city on 3 May 1644, and the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 ended the empire.
mvt.academic.sync: Louis-Napoleon made himself Emperor Napoleon III on 2 December 1852 and set Haussmann to rebuild Paris from 1853; the Palais Garnier was among the new monuments. Baudelaire and his publisher were prosecuted for Les Fleurs du mal in 1857, and in 1863 his Painter of Modern Life defined modernity as ‘the transitory, the fugitive, the contingent’. Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, the Franco-Prussian War ended the Second Empire in 1870, and the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 divided Africa.
mvt.impressionism.o.0.what: Monet’s Impression, Sunrise, 1872, which gave the movement its name
mvt.impressionism.o.1.what: Renoir’s Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette, 1876, Degas’s The Ballet Class, c. 1875, and Manet’s Olympia, 1863
mvt.impressionism.o.2.what: Monet’s Woman with a Parasol, 1875, and Cassatt’s The Boating Party, c. 1894
mvt.impressionism.o.3.what: Renoir’s Luncheon of the Boating Party, c. 1881
mvt.impressionism.o.4.what: Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère, 1882
mvt.impressionism.sync: Napoleon III abdicated after the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71, which unified Germany and brought the Third Republic; Haussmann’s boulevards had remade Paris since 1853. Japan’s Meiji Restoration came in 1868, and from the 1870s Japonisme carried its prints into the Paris studios. The first telephone call was made in 1876, Edison patented a practical light bulb in 1879 and Karl Benz sold the first commercial motor car in 1886. The Berlin Conference of 1884–85 carved up Africa.
mvt.postimpressionism.o.0.what: Seurat’s A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, c. 1884, Cézanne’s The Basket of Apples, c. 1893, and Toulouse-Lautrec’s At the Moulin Rouge, c. 1895
mvt.postimpressionism.o.1.what: Gauguin’s Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?, c. 1898
mvt.postimpressionism.sync: Karl Benz sold the first commercial motor car in 1886, and millions came to the Paris expositions and the new Eiffel Tower. Freud published The Interpretation of Dreams in Vienna in 1899, the year the Boxer Rebellion broke out in China; the Wright Flyer flew in 1903. Japan beat Russia in the war of 1904–05, which set off the Russian Revolution of 1905, and in the same year Einstein published special relativity and the equation of mass and energy.
mvt.symbolism.o.1.what: Franz von Stuck’s The Wild Chase, c. 1889
mvt.symbolism.o.2.what: Klimt’s The Kiss, c. 1908, described as both Symbolism and early Expressionism
mvt.symbolism.sync: The Berlin Conference of 1884–85 divided Africa among the European powers, and Karl Benz sold the first motor car in 1886. Freud published The Interpretation of Dreams in Vienna in 1899, and the Boxer Rebellion was put down by eight nations in 1901. Paris drew millions to its expositions and the Eiffel Tower. Japan defeated Russia in 1904–05, the Russian Revolution of 1905 followed, and Einstein published special relativity the same year.
mvt.artsandcrafts.sync: The Great Exhibition opened in the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park on 1 May 1851, and the Museum of Manufactures, forerunner of the Victoria and Albert Museum, opened at Marlborough House in 1852. Edison patented a practical light bulb in 1879, large electric utilities followed from 1882 and Karl Benz sold the first motor car in 1886. The Berlin Conference of 1884–85 divided Africa, the Wiener Werkstätte was founded in Vienna in 1903, and the First World War began in 1914.
mvt.viennasecession.o.2.what: the group’s own exhibition house, built in 1898, a year after the Secession was founded in April 1897
mvt.viennasecession.sync: The Secession was founded in April 1897, and its building and the Stadtbahn opened in 1898. Freud’s The Interpretation of Dreams was published in Vienna on 4 November 1899, the year the magazine Die Fackel began. The Wiener Werkstätte followed in 1903 and the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society in 1908. The First World War began in 1914, Franz Joseph I was buried on 30 November 1916, and defeat in 1918 opened the years of Red Vienna.
mvt.miriskusstva.sync: Nicholas II was crowned in 1896, and the Moscow Art Theatre was founded in 1898. Japan defeated Russia in 1904–05, and Bloody Sunday in January 1905 opened the revolution that brought the St Petersburg Soviet. Akhmatova joined the Acmeists around 1910, published Evening in 1912 and frequented the Stray Dog cabaret. The capital was renamed Petrograd in 1914, and after 1917 between 900,000 and 2 million Russians emigrated; Bakst, Diaghilev, Pavlova and Nijinsky were among the émigrés.
mvt.fauvism.o.0.n: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art
mvt.fauvism.o.0.what: Matisse’s Woman with a Hat, 1905, shown at the Salon d’Automne that named the Fauves
mvt.fauvism.o.1.what: Matisse’s Portrait of Madame Matisse (The Green Stripe), 1905
mvt.fauvism.o.3.n: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
mvt.fauvism.sync: The Wright Flyer had flown in 1903. Japan and Russia fought over Manchuria and Korea in 1904–05, and the defeat set off the Russian Revolution of 1905, a wave of mass unrest across the empire. In 1905 Einstein published special relativity and the equation of mass and energy. Louis Vauxcelles named the Fauves at the Salon d’Automne that autumn; by 1907 they no longer shocked anyone, and Picasso was painting Les Demoiselles d’Avignon.
mvt.expressionism.o.0.what: Kirchner’s Portrait of Erich Heckel at the Easel, c. 1907, from Die Brücke
mvt.expressionism.o.1.what: Jawlensky’s Portrait of Alexander Sakharoff, 1909, from the circle of Der Blaue Reiter
mvt.expressionism.o.2.n: Museum of Modern Art, New York
mvt.expressionism.o.3.what: Beckmann’s The Night, 1919, from the reaction against Expressionism
mvt.expressionism.sync: Die Brücke formed in Dresden in 1905, the year of the first Russian revolution and of Einstein’s special relativity; Der Blaue Reiter lasted from 1911 to 1914, and Kandinsky published Concerning the Spiritual in Art in 1911. In 1914 the First World War began; it killed up to 17 million people by 1918, and Einstein proposed general relativity in the middle of it, in 1915. The Expressionists worked largely between that war and the next.
mvt.cubism.o.0.n: Museum of Modern Art, New York
mvt.cubism.o.0.what: Picasso’s Les Demoiselles d’Avignon, painted in Paris in June–July 1907
mvt.cubism.o.1.n: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art
mvt.cubism.o.1.what: Braque’s Violin and Candlestick, 1910, analytic Cubism
mvt.cubism.o.2.what: Juan Gris’s Portrait of Pablo Picasso, 1912, and Léger’s The Railway Crossing, 1919
mvt.cubism.o.3.what: Robert Delaunay’s Simultaneous Windows on the City, 1912, Orphism
mvt.cubism.sync: Picasso painted Les Demoiselles d’Avignon in Paris in the summer of 1907, four years after the Wright Flyer’s first flight and two after Einstein’s special relativity. Russia was still shaken by its defeat by Japan and the revolution of 1905. Kandinsky published Concerning the Spiritual in Art in 1911, and Duchamp became famous after the Armory Show in New York in 1913. The First World War broke out in 1914 and killed up to 17 million people by 1918.
mvt.futurism.sync: The poet Marinetti founded Futurism in the first decade of flight: the Wright Flyer had flown in 1903. The First World War of 1914–18 killed up to 17 million people; Boccioni died in 1916, in the middle of it. The Bolsheviks took Russia in 1917, influenza killed between 17 and 100 million in 1918–19, and fascism gained ground in Italy, Germany and Spain through the 1920s. The Great Depression began in 1929, Franco rebelled in 1936 and the Second World War began in 1939.
mvt.russianavantgarde.sync: Malevich founded Suprematism, an art of ‘the supremacy of pure artistic feeling’, and Rodchenko and Tatlin founded Constructivism. Petrograd took that name in 1914; the February Revolution of 1917 was followed by the October Revolution, and in March 1918 Moscow became the capital. The Comintern held its founding congress there in 1919, the Lenin Mausoleum was built in 1924, the year Petrograd became Leningrad, Kirov was assassinated in 1934 and the Moscow Metro opened on 15 May 1935.
mvt.dada.o.0.what: Hannah Höch’s Cut with the Kitchen Knife through the Last Epoch of Weimar Beer-Belly Culture in Germany, 1919
mvt.dada.o.2.what: Duchamp’s The Bride Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors, Even (The Large Glass), c. 1923
mvt.dada.sync: Dada began in neutral Zürich during the First World War, which killed up to 17 million people between 1914 and 1918. The Bolsheviks set up the first communist state in 1917, and the influenza pandemic of 1918–19 killed between 17 and 100 million. Germany became the Weimar Republic; Hitler’s Beer Hall Putsch failed in 1923, and fascism gained ground in Italy, Germany and Spain. By 1923 Duchamp had given up art for chess.
mvt.destijl.o.0.n: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
mvt.destijl.o.0.what: Paul Klee’s Tale à la Hoffmann, 1921, from his Bauhaus years
mvt.destijl.sync: Mondrian, a Theosophist, set out Neo-Plasticism with De Stijl, and Constructivism reached the Bauhaus painters. Paris drew artists from around the world between the wars and reached its peak population of 2.1 million in 1921. Germany became the Weimar Republic, Hitler’s Beer Hall Putsch failed in 1923, and the Great Depression began in 1929. Einstein left Nazi Germany for Princeton in 1933, and the Nazis condemned modern art as degenerate and promoted heroic realism.
mvt.surrealism.o.0.n: Museum of Modern Art, New York
mvt.surrealism.o.0.what: Dalí’s The Persistence of Memory, 1931, and de Chirico’s The Song of Love, 1914
mvt.surrealism.o.1.n: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
mvt.surrealism.o.2.n: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
mvt.surrealism.o.3.what: André Masson’s Pedestal Table in the Studio, 1922
mvt.surrealism.o.4.n: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Madrid
mvt.surrealism.sync: André Breton published the Surrealist Manifesto in 1924, drawing on Freud, whose Interpretation of Dreams had appeared in Vienna in 1899. The Great Depression began in 1929, Einstein left Nazi Germany for Princeton in 1933, and the Nazis condemned modern art as degenerate. Franco rebelled against the Spanish Republic in 1936, the year of the London International Surrealist Exhibition, and Picasso answered the war with Guernica. Freud fled Vienna for London in 1938, and the Second World War began in 1939.
mvt.artdeco.o.0.what: the building itself, constructed in 1930, in situ
mvt.artdeco.o.1.what: the building itself, built in 1931, in situ
mvt.artdeco.o.2.what: the complex itself, built by 1939, in situ
mvt.artdeco.sync: Paris was the capital of modern art between the wars and reached its peak population of 2.1 million in 1921. MoMA opened in New York in November 1929, as the Great Depression began. The Chrysler Building went up in 1930 and the Empire State Building in 1931. Fascism gained ground in Italy, Germany and Spain, Einstein left Nazi Germany in 1933, Franco rebelled against the Spanish Republic in 1936, and the Second World War began in 1939.
mvt.mexicanmuralism.sync: The Mexican Revolution of 1910–20 reached the capital: Villa and Zapata briefly held it, and Huerta’s coup of February 1913, the Decena Trágica, ousted Madero, who was killed. The Secretariat of Public Education made its headquarters in the city in 1921, the Palacio de Bellas Artes was inaugurated in 1934 and the Taller de Gráfica Popular founded in 1937. Trotsky was assassinated there on 21 August 1940, the university city was built in 1954, and the Tlatelolco massacre came on 2 October 1968.
mvt.harlemrenaissance.sync: In the first Great Migration, from 1910 to 1940, about 1.6 million Black Americans left the rural South for the industrial North, drawn by wartime labour shortages and driven by Jim Crow laws and the boll weevil, and Caribbean immigrants also fed the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s. The Armory Show brought modern art to New York in 1913, the First World War ended in 1918, MoMA opened in 1929 as the Depression began, and Jacob Lawrence’s Migration Series was shown at MoMA in 1941.
mvt.abex.o.1.n: Private collection of Steven A. Cohen
mvt.abex.sync: The Second World War ended with the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945, the year the United Nations was founded. The Cold War began in 1947, Israel was created in 1948 and the People’s Republic of China in 1949, and Korea was at war from 1950 to 1953. Robert Coates coined ‘abstract expressionism’ in 1946, and the Irascibles boycotted the Metropolitan Museum’s exhibition American Painting Today – 1950.
mvt.colorfield.sync: Greenberg grouped Rothko, Newman and Still as Colour Field painters, and Louis and Noland formed the Washington Color School. The Korean War ran from 1950 to 1953 and the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957. In 1959 the Guggenheim’s new building opened in New York and MoMA’s ‘16 Americans’ showed Stella’s stripes. The Cuban Missile Crisis brought the superpowers to the brink, and US Marines landed near Da Nang in March 1965.
mvt.gutai.sync: The American raid of 9–10 March 1945 killed more than 100,000 people in Tokyo, and the US occupation under MacArthur lasted until 1952; the Tokyo War Crimes Tribunal opened in 1946. The Korean War ran from 1950 to 1953 and Sputnik flew in 1957. The economic miracle and the 1964 Olympics rebuilt the capital, and the Tōkaidō Shinkansen began service that year. Tokyo passed a pollution-control ordinance in 1969, and Zengakuren students marched over Okinawa in 1971.
mvt.cobra.sync: Germany occupied Paris from 1940 to 1944, and the Fourth Republic followed in 1946. Camus published The Stranger in 1942 and The Plague in 1947, Sartre, Beauvoir and Merleau-Ponty founded Les Temps modernes in October 1945, and The Second Sex appeared in 1949. Dubuffet coined ‘art brut’ just after the war. The Cold War began in 1947, the People’s Republic of China was founded in 1949, and The Rebel of 1951 ended Camus’s friendship with Sartre.
mvt.pop.o.0.n: Museum of Modern Art, New York
mvt.pop.sync: Lawrence Alloway first used the term ‘Pop Art’ in 1956, and Warhol opened his first Factory in New York in 1962. The Soviet Union had launched Sputnik in 1957; the Cuban Missile Crisis brought the superpowers to the brink, and US Marines landed near Da Nang in March 1965. The Tet Offensive of January 1968 hurt American support for the war, Czechoslovakia had its Prague Spring that year, and Apollo 11 landed on the Moon in 1969.
mvt.minimalism.sync: Stella’s stripe paintings appeared in MoMA’s ‘16 Americans’ in 1959, Judd wrote ‘Specific Objects’ in 1964, and Michael Fried attacked Robert Morris in ‘Art and Objecthood’ in 1967. US strength in Vietnam peaked at about 543,400 troops in April 1969, the year Apollo 11 landed on the Moon. National Guardsmen killed students at Kent State in May 1970, the Paris Peace Accords were signed in January 1973, and after the Yom Kippur War OPEC used an oil embargo.
mvt.conceptual.sync: Warhol opened his first Factory in 1962. After the Gulf of Tonkin incident of August 1964 Congress passed its resolution, and US Marines landed near Da Nang in March 1965. The Tet Offensive of January 1968 hurt American support for the war, Czechoslovakia had its Prague Spring, and the Stonewall riot of 1969 helped start the modern gay rights movement in the year of Apollo 11. The Paris Peace Accords followed in 1973, and then OPEC’s oil embargo.
mvt.arteprovera.sync: The Tet Offensive of January 1968 hurt American support for the war in Vietnam, and Czechoslovakia had its Prague Spring the same year. US strength in Vietnam peaked at about 543,400 troops in April 1969, and Apollo 11 landed on the Moon that year. National Guardsmen killed students at Kent State in May 1970. The Paris Peace Accords were signed on 27 January 1973, and after the Yom Kippur War OPEC used an oil embargo that opened the energy crisis.
mvt.monoha.sync: Tokyo had rebuilt for the 1964 Olympics and the Tōkaidō Shinkansen. The high-rise Kasumigaseki Building was finished in 1968, and the city passed a pollution-control ordinance in 1969. Zengakuren students demonstrated in 1971 against the terms of Okinawa’s return, and the Nakagin Capsule Tower went up in 1972. Abroad the Tet Offensive of 1968, Apollo 11 in 1969, the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 and OPEC’s oil embargo after the Yom Kippur War framed the years.
mvt.dansaekhwa.sync: Seoul changed hands four times in the Korean War of 1950–53 and was largely destroyed, and refugees swelled it to about 2.5 million. It annexed the towns around it in 1963, and the industrialisation of the 1960s and 1970s raised living standards sharply. By 1980 the city held 8,364,379 people, a high-rise building boom followed, and in 1988 Seoul hosted the Olympics and opened the Seoul Museum of Art. Abroad, OPEC’s oil embargo of 1973 and the fall of Saigon in 1975 marked the decade.
mvt.photorealism.sync: US forces left Vietnam by March 1973 and Saigon fell on 30 April 1975. After the Yom Kippur War of 1973 OPEC’s oil embargo opened the energy crisis. In New York the twin towers of the World Trade Center were completed on 4 April 1973, the Daily News ran ‘Ford to City: Drop Dead’ on 30 October 1975, Studio 54 opened in April 1977, and a blackout that July was followed by rioting and looting.
mvt.neoexpressionism.sync: Martial law was imposed in Poland in 1981, the year the CDC reported the first cases of what became AIDS; New York had the most American cases. Western painting counts Basquiat, Haring and Schnabel among the American neo-expressionists and Richter and Kiefer among the European ones. The Chernobyl reactor exploded in 1986, the Dia Center for the Arts opened in New York in 1987, and in 1989 revolutions freed Eastern and Central Europe while protesters filled Tiananmen Square.
mvt.pictures.sync: The work came after New York’s fiscal crisis of 1975, when the Daily News ran ‘Ford to City: Drop Dead’, and the blackout of July 1977 with its rioting and looting. The CDC reported the first AIDS cases in June 1981, and New York had the most American cases. Martial law came to Poland in 1981, the Chernobyl reactor exploded in 1986, the Dia Center for the Arts opened in 1987, and the revolutions of 1989 freed Eastern and Central Europe.
mvt.yba.sync: The revolutions of 1989 freed Eastern and Central Europe, Germany reunited in 1990 and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991; the Rwandan genocide followed in 1994, and Japan sank into its Lost Decades. In London Tate Modern opened in the former Bankside Power Station in May 2000, with the London Eye and the swaying Millennium Bridge, and in 2011 it showed Damien Hirst’s For the Love of God. Four suicide bombers killed 56 people on London’s transport on 7 July 2005.
mvt.chinesecontemporary.sync: Protesters filled Tiananmen Square in Beijing in 1989, the year revolutions freed Eastern Europe, and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991. Lehman Brothers went bankrupt on 15 September 2008 and the financial crisis followed. Ai Weiwei filled the Turbine Hall of Tate Modern with Sunflower Seeds from October 2010 to April 2011. COVID-19, identified in Wuhan in December 2019, was declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020, and the WHO estimates 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020–21.
mvt.indianmodern.sync: Pakistan became a dominion on 14 August 1947 and India on 15 August. The Radcliffe Line, revealed on 17 August, displaced an estimated 12 to 20 million people, and most scholars accept about a million dead, above all in Punjab and Bengal. New Delhi, the capital Lutyens inaugurated in 1931, became the capital of India in 1947 and hosted the Asian Games in 1951 and 1982. The Cold War ran from 1947 until the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
mvt.africanmodern.sync: Lagos opened an Art Exhibition Centre and museum in 1943 and founded the Nigerian National Museum in 1957, and most colonised African and Asian countries won independence in the second half of the century. The University of Lagos opened in 1962. FESTAC ’77, the Second World African Festival of Arts and Culture, was held in Lagos in 1977, the federal government moved to Abuja in 1991, and El Anatsui filled the Turbine Hall of Tate Modern in 2023–24.
mvt.streetart.sync: New York’s fiscal crisis peaked when the Daily News ran ‘Ford to City: Drop Dead’ on 30 October 1975, and the blackout of July 1977 brought rioting and looting that devastated Bushwick. The first AIDS reports came in 1981, the twin towers fell on 11 September 2001, Lehman Brothers failed on 15 September 2008 and Occupy Wall Street began on 17 September 2011. In August 2024 Banksy’s ninth and final animal in a London series appeared on the gates of London Zoo.
mvt.digital.sync: Turing described his universal machine in 1936, designed the Automatic Computing Engine in 1945–46 and proposed the imitation game, the Turing test. Apollo 11 reached the Moon in 1969 and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991. Lehman Brothers failed in September 2008. COVID-19 was declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020 and London went into lockdown on 23 March; Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February 2022, and UNHCR recorded about 7.8 million Ukrainian refugees in Europe that November.
mvt.ultracontemporary.sync: COVID-19, identified in Wuhan in December 2019, was declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020; the WHO estimates 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020–21, and the Tokyo Olympics of 2020 were held in 2021. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, and by September 2025 UNHCR counted 5.7 million Ukrainian refugees worldwide, about 90% of them in Europe. Queen Elizabeth II died on 8 September 2022, and Banksy’s last London animal appeared at the zoo in August 2024.
mvt.superflat.sync: Japan sank into the economic stagnation of its Lost Decades in the 1990s. Tokyo’s metropolitan government moved to a new building in Shinjuku in 1991, and the Tokyo subway sarin attack came on 20 March 1995. The Tokyo International Anime Fair began in 2002. The Great East Japan earthquake and tsunami of 11 March 2011 crippled the Fukushima nuclear plant, and the 2020 Olympics, postponed by COVID-19, were held in Tokyo in 2021.
